quizzes.title: The basic economic problem quiz
quizzes.description: Retrieve the sequence: infinite wants, finite resources, scarcity, choice and the basic economic problem.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a want?
choices: Something a person would like to have, use or experience.
Something a person already owns.
Only something needed for survival.
Only a physical product sold in a shop.
questions.explanation: A want may be a good, service or experience that a person would like to have or use.

questions.prompt: Human wants are described as __________ because they continue and develop.
questions.explanation: Infinite and unlimited are both accepted descriptions of human wants.

questions.prompt: What does “infinite wants” mean?
choices: Human wants continue and new wants can appear after others are satisfied.
Every individual wants every product that exists.
No human want can ever be satisfied.
Only people with low incomes have wants.
questions.explanation: Infinite wants means that the process of wanting continues, not that every person wants every product.

questions.prompt: The productive resources available at any moment are __________ rather than endless.
questions.explanation: Productive resources are finite or limited in amount. They are also called factors of production.

questions.prompt: Which option contains productive resources rather than a want?
choices: Workers, flour and ovens used by a bakery
Customers’ wish for more bread
A class’s wish for a larger sports centre
A family’s wish for a holiday
questions.explanation: Workers, flour and ovens are inputs used to produce bread, so they are productive resources, also called factors of production. The other options state wants.

questions.prompt: When infinite wants exceed the finite resources available to satisfy them, there is __________.
questions.explanation: Scarcity is the relationship created when wants exceed the resources available.

questions.prompt: Why can scarcity exist when supermarket shelves are full?
choices: The products still require finite resources, while human wants continue.
Full shelves mean that every want has been satisfied.
Scarcity means only that one product is temporarily unavailable.
Resources become unlimited once goods reach a shop.
questions.explanation: Scarcity is not an empty shelf. It is the continuing relationship between infinite wants and finite resources.

questions.prompt: Scarcity makes economic __________ unavoidable.
questions.explanation: Finite resources must be allocated between alternative uses, so a choice is necessary.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines the basic economic problem?
choices: Scarcity of finite resources compared with unlimited human wants.
Some consumers have lower incomes than others.
Shops sometimes run out of products.
Governments sometimes spend too much.
questions.explanation: The basic economic problem is the scarcity of finite resources compared with unlimited wants.

questions.prompt: What does economics study?
choices: How consumers, workers, firms and governments make choices when resources are finite and wants are infinite.
How to make every person equally wealthy.
How to predict every future price exactly.
How shops prevent products from selling out.
questions.explanation: Economics studies choices about using finite resources when not every want can be satisfied.

quizzes.title: Factors of production and rewards quiz
quizzes.description: Identify land, labour, capital and enterprise, then match each factor with its reward.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a factor of production?
choices: A resource or input used to produce goods and services.
Any product that a consumer wants to buy.
Only a machine used inside a factory.
Money kept in a business bank account.
questions.explanation: A factor of production is any resource or input used in the production process.

questions.prompt: Natural resources used in production are called __________.
questions.explanation: Land includes all natural resources used in production, not only the ground.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of the factor of production land?
choices: Fish in the sea caught for food
A fishing boat made in a shipyard
A fisher’s human effort
The owner who organises the fishing business
questions.explanation: Fish are a natural resource. The boat is capital, the effort is labour and the organiser supplies enterprise.

questions.prompt: Human effort or workers used in production are called __________.
questions.explanation: Labour includes both physical and mental human effort.

questions.prompt: Which item is capital?
choices: A sewing machine used in a clothing factory
Cotton growing in a field
A worker sewing a shirt
Cash in a consumer’s wallet
questions.explanation: The sewing machine is a human-made good used in production.

questions.prompt: What does enterprise contribute to production?
choices: It organises the other factors and takes risks.
It provides only natural resources.
It provides only physical human effort.
It turns every machine into money.
questions.explanation: Enterprise coordinates land, labour and capital and accepts business risk.

questions.prompt: The reward for land is __________.
questions.explanation: Rent is the reward for supplying land or natural resources.

questions.prompt: The reward for labour is wages or __________.
questions.explanation: Workers receive wages or salaries for supplying labour.

questions.prompt: The reward for capital is __________.
questions.explanation: Interest is the reward for supplying capital.

questions.prompt: The reward for enterprise is __________.
questions.explanation: Profit rewards the entrepreneur for organising production and taking risks.

quizzes.title: Market economic system quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 2.8.1: market forces, private sector ownership, the price mechanism and profit motive.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a market economic system?
choices: Resources are allocated mainly by market forces or the price mechanism, with private sector ownership and the profit motive.
The government owns all resources and sets all output.
All goods are provided free by the public sector.
Firms produce only what the government orders.
questions.explanation: This matches the definitions source: market forces / price mechanism, private sector ownership and decisions influenced by the profit motive.

questions.prompt: A market economic system includes private __________ of resources.
questions.explanation: Private ownership is a core feature of a market economy.

questions.prompt: Prices act as signals and incentives through the price __________.
questions.explanation: The price mechanism uses price changes to allocate resources.

questions.prompt: Why is profit important in a market economy?
choices: It gives firms an incentive to produce goods consumers want.
It guarantees equal income.
It removes external costs.
It means government owns firms.
questions.explanation: Profit is an incentive that can move resources towards demanded goods.

questions.prompt: A coffee shop owned by shareholders is in the...
choices: private sector
public sector
planned sector
tax sector
questions.explanation: The private sector includes firms owned by individuals or shareholders.

questions.prompt: Which economy combines private-sector market activity with public-sector intervention?
choices: Mixed economy
Pure market economy
Budget deficit
Current account
questions.explanation: A mixed economy uses both markets and government intervention.

questions.prompt: Market forces means demand and __________.
questions.explanation: Demand and supply influence prices in markets.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to allocate resources?
choices: Decide how land, labour, capital and enterprise are used.
Print more money.
Measure inflation only.
Ban all trade.
questions.explanation: Allocation means deciding how scarce resources are used.

quizzes.title: Price mechanism quiz
quizzes.description: Check demand and supply signals, incentives and resource allocation.

questions.prompt: In a market economy, prices act as signals and __________.
questions.explanation: Prices signal scarcity and create incentives for buyers and sellers.

questions.prompt: If demand rises and supply is unchanged, what is the likely short-run effect?
choices: Price rises and profit may rise.
Price must fall to zero.
Government owns the market.
Resources leave immediately.
questions.explanation: Higher demand tends to raise price and profit incentives.

questions.prompt: Which chain best shows resources moving into a market?
choices: Demand rises -> price rises -> profit rises -> firms use more resources.
Demand rises -> profit falls -> firms leave.
Demand rises -> prices disappear.
Demand rises -> supply is banned.
questions.explanation: Profit signals attract land, labour, capital and enterprise.

questions.prompt: When demand falls, price and profit may __________.
questions.explanation: Falling demand sends a signal to reduce output.

questions.prompt: Consumer __________ means firms produce what consumers demand.
questions.explanation: Consumer sovereignty means spending decisions influence production.

questions.prompt: Demand for electric cars rises. What should firms do if profit rises?
choices: Allocate more resources to electric car production.
Ignore consumer demand.
Produce fewer electric cars.
Stop using prices.
questions.explanation: Rising profit encourages more resources into production.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only factors of production?
choices: Land, labour, capital and enterprise
Imports, exports, taxes and subsidies
Inflation, money, prices and GDP
Choice, equality, monopoly and pollution
questions.explanation: These are the resources allocated by the price mechanism.

questions.prompt: The price mechanism allocates resources through changes in __________.
questions.explanation: Price changes signal where resources should move.

quizzes.title: Arguments for markets quiz
quizzes.description: Check choice, incentives and efficiency.

questions.prompt: Which list gives syllabus arguments for markets?
choices: Choice, incentives and efficiency
Inequality, market failure and under-provision
Taxes, spending and borrowing
Inflation, deflation and unemployment
questions.explanation: The syllabus names choice, incentives and efficiency as advantages.

questions.prompt: Competition between many firms can increase consumer __________.
questions.explanation: Choice is a key argument for markets.

questions.prompt: How can profit encourage innovation?
choices: Better products may attract consumers and increase sales.
Profit prevents firms from improving products.
Profit guarantees equality.
Profit means prices never change.
questions.explanation: Profit gives firms an incentive to improve products.

questions.prompt: Competition can pressure firms to reduce waste and lower __________.
questions.explanation: This can improve efficiency.

questions.prompt: A large app market with many developers most directly shows...
choices: consumer choice and innovation
non-provision of public goods
higher external costs only
a planned economy
questions.explanation: Many developers and apps can increase choice and innovation.

questions.prompt: When EV firms compete to improve batteries and prices, this shows...
choices: incentives and innovation
under-consumption of merit goods
no role for prices
public ownership of all resources
questions.explanation: Competition and profit can create incentives to innovate.

questions.prompt: Firms may improve logistics to reduce waste and become more __________.
questions.explanation: Efficiency means using fewer resources for the same or greater output.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest exam chain?
choices: Competition pressures firms to cut costs, which may lower prices for consumers.
Markets are good because markets are good.
Choice is bad because firms exist.
Prices do not matter in markets.
questions.explanation: The strongest answer gives a cause and consequence.

quizzes.title: Arguments against markets quiz
quizzes.description: Check inequality, market failure and under-provision.

questions.prompt: Which list gives syllabus arguments against markets?
choices: Inequality, market failure and under-provision of some goods
Choice, incentives and efficiency only
Exports, imports and exchange rates
Money supply, interest rates and inflation
questions.explanation: The syllabus names inequality, market failure and under-provision.

questions.prompt: Market demand reflects wants and ability to __________.
questions.explanation: Richer consumers have more spending power.

questions.prompt: A factory pollutes and nearby residents face health costs. What is ignored?
choices: External costs
Consumer sovereignty
Higher choice
Private ownership only
questions.explanation: Pollution imposes costs on third parties.

questions.prompt: Market failure means resources are allocated __________ by the market.
questions.explanation: Market failure is inefficient allocation by the market.

questions.prompt: Why might street lighting be under-provided by private firms?
choices: People can benefit without paying.
It has no social benefit.
Prices always allocate it perfectly.
It is a luxury private good.
questions.explanation: Free riders make it difficult to charge users.

questions.prompt: Public goods may suffer from under-__________ or non-provision.
questions.explanation: Some socially useful goods may not be provided by markets.

questions.prompt: A balanced answer about markets should...
choices: Use arguments for and against before judging.
Only list advantages.
Only list disadvantages.
Avoid examples.
questions.explanation: Discuss questions need both sides and a judgement.

questions.prompt: Which chain is strongest?
choices: External cost ignored -> market price too low -> output may be too high.
External cost ignored -> choice must rise.
Pollution -> no market failure.
Public goods -> profit must rise.
questions.explanation: This explains the mechanism and consequence.

quizzes.title: External costs and benefits quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 2.9 externalities, private effects and social effects.

questions.prompt: What is market failure?
choices: An inefficient allocation of resources by the market.
Any fall in a firm profit.
A market where prices never change.
A situation where consumers always have too much choice.
questions.explanation: Market failure is inefficient allocation or misallocation of resources by the market.

questions.prompt: Social cost equals private cost plus external __________.
questions.explanation: External costs are added to private costs.

questions.prompt: Social benefit equals private benefit plus external __________.
questions.explanation: External benefits are added to private benefits.

questions.prompt: Which is an external cost?
choices: Dirty air suffered by nearby residents from a factory.
The wage paid to a worker.
The rent paid by a shop.
The price paid by the buyer.
questions.explanation: An external cost is suffered by a third party.

questions.prompt: Which is an external benefit?
choices: Lower disease spread after people are vaccinated.
The price paid for the vaccine.
A firm rent payment.
A consumer private shopping benefit only.
questions.explanation: An external benefit is gained by third parties who are not directly involved in the transaction.

questions.prompt: An externality affects a third __________.
questions.explanation: Third parties are outside the direct buyer-seller transaction.

questions.prompt: If external costs are ignored, what may happen to market output?
choices: It may be too high from society viewpoint.
It must be exactly efficient.
It will always be zero.
It will always be too low.
questions.explanation: When social cost exceeds private cost, the market may produce or consume too much.

questions.prompt: If external benefits are ignored, what may happen to market output?
choices: It may be too low from society viewpoint.
It must be exactly efficient.
It will always be too high.
It will always be a public good.
questions.explanation: When social benefit exceeds private benefit, the market may produce or consume too little.

quizzes.title: Merit and demerit goods quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 2.9 merit goods, demerit goods, under-consumption and over-consumption.

questions.prompt: What is a merit good?
choices: A beneficial good that may be under-consumed.
A harmful good that is over-consumed.
A non-rival and non-excludable good.
A good supplied by only one firm.
questions.explanation: Merit goods are beneficial and may be under-consumed because people do not recognise their full benefits.

questions.prompt: What is a demerit good?
choices: A harmful good that may be over-consumed.
A good that always has no price.
A good that cannot be excluded.
A good that is always exported.
questions.explanation: Demerit goods may be over-consumed when people do not appreciate their full costs.

questions.prompt: Merit goods may be under-__________.
questions.explanation: Consumers may demand too little because they do not realise the full benefits.

questions.prompt: Demerit goods may be over-__________.
questions.explanation: Consumers may demand too much because they do not realise the full costs.

questions.prompt: Why may education be under-consumed in a free market?
choices: Consumers may not realise long-term benefits or be unable to afford enough.
It has no social benefit.
It is always harmful.
It is a monopoly by definition.
questions.explanation: Education is a merit good whose long-term benefits may not be fully recognised.

questions.prompt: Why may tobacco be over-consumed in a free market?
choices: Consumers may underestimate addiction and long-term health costs.
It is a public good.
It creates only benefits.
It is always under-consumed.
questions.explanation: Tobacco is a demerit good because consumers may not fully recognise its costs.

questions.prompt: Which is usually treated as a merit good?
choices: Healthcare
Tobacco
Gambling
A monopoly rail service
questions.explanation: Healthcare is beneficial and may be under-consumed if consumers do not recognise its full benefits.

questions.prompt: Which is usually treated as a demerit good?
choices: Tobacco
Education
Vaccination
Street lighting
questions.explanation: Tobacco is harmful and may be over-consumed if consumers do not recognise its full costs.

quizzes.title: Public goods quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 2.9 public goods, free riders, private revenue and non-provision.

questions.prompt: Which pair of features defines a public good?
choices: Non-rival and non-excludable.
Expensive and imported.
Harmful and addictive.
Produced by one firm.
questions.explanation: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable, so it needs to be financed by government.

questions.prompt: What does non-rival mean?
choices: One person using the good does not reduce use by others.
Only one person can use the good.
Non-payers can always be excluded.
The good is always harmful.
questions.explanation: Non-rival means consumption by one user does not reduce availability to others.

questions.prompt: What does non-excludable mean?
choices: Non-payers cannot easily be stopped from benefiting.
The good is always produced abroad.
The good has no social benefit.
Only rich people can use the good.
questions.explanation: Non-excludable means it is difficult to prevent non-payers from benefiting.

questions.prompt: What is the free-rider problem?
choices: People can benefit without paying.
People always pay more tax.
Firms always innovate.
Consumers always buy too much education.
questions.explanation: Free riders make it difficult for private firms to charge every beneficiary.

questions.prompt: Weak private revenue may lead to non-__________.
questions.explanation: Markets may not provide public goods because private revenue may be too low to cover costs and make a profit.

questions.prompt: Which is the best public good example?
choices: Flood protection for a town
A sandwich
A private tutoring lesson
A cigarette
questions.explanation: Flood protection can be non-rival and non-excludable when many homes are protected together.

questions.prompt: Which feature normally helps private firms sell private goods?
choices: Excludability
Free-rider problem
Non-provision
No price possible
questions.explanation: If buyers can be excluded unless they pay, firms can earn private revenue.

questions.prompt: Why is a merit good not automatically a public good?
choices: A merit good can often be sold to individual consumers.
A merit good is always harmful.
A public good is always over-consumed.
A merit good must have no benefits.
questions.explanation: Many merit goods, such as education, are excludable even though consumers may not fully recognise their benefits.

quizzes.title: Monopoly power and evaluation quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 2.9 monopoly power, restricted supply and evaluation.

questions.prompt: How can monopoly power cause market failure?
choices: A firm may restrict output and charge higher prices.
Competition always increases.
Prices become unnecessary.
Consumers always gain more choice.
questions.explanation: Abuse of monopoly power can restrict supply and harm consumers.

questions.prompt: A monopoly may restrict output and charge higher __________.
questions.explanation: Restricted supply can push prices up.

questions.prompt: What may happen to consumer choice when competition is weak?
choices: Choice may fall.
Choice must increase.
Choice becomes unlimited.
Choice is unrelated to market failure.
questions.explanation: A dominant firm may offer less variety or weaker quality.

questions.prompt: Which is a possible benefit of a large monopoly firm?
choices: Economies of scale may lower costs.
It always harms consumers.
It always removes all external costs.
It always creates free riders.
questions.explanation: Evaluation should recognise possible economies of scale or innovation.

questions.prompt: Public goods may suffer from non-__________.
questions.explanation: This reviews another type of market failure.

questions.prompt: Demerit goods may be over-__________.
questions.explanation: This reviews over-consumption.

questions.prompt: Which phrase completes the external cost explanation?
choices: Social cost exceeds private cost.
Social benefit is zero.
Private cost exceeds every social cost.
No third party is affected.
questions.explanation: External costs mean social cost is greater than private cost.

questions.prompt: A discuss answer should end with a reasoned __________.
questions.explanation: A judgement weighs the arguments.

quizzes.title: Money: forms and functions quiz
quizzes.description: Retrieval of the definition, forms and four functions taught in class 1.

questions.prompt: Which definition of money is correct?
choices: Anything scarce that rises in value.
Anything generally accepted as a means of payment.
Any device that can open a banking app.
Any asset owned by a household.
questions.explanation: Money must be generally accepted and able to settle payments. A phone may move money, but is not itself money.

questions.prompt: A customer taps a debit card to pay. What is the money in this transaction?
choices: The plastic card.
The card reader.
The bank deposit transferred between accounts.
The receipt printed by the shop.
questions.explanation: The card and reader are payment tools. The bank deposit is the value transferred to settle the payment.

questions.prompt: One function of money is to act as a measure of value. What does this mean?
choices: Money allows people to borrow and lend.
Money allows people to save surplus income.
Money is used to buy goods and services.
Money is used to compare the worth of different goods and services.
questions.explanation: A measure of value is the unit-of-account function. A common unit lets people compare worth. Source: 0455_s23_12 Q12.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Original recent Paper 1 question; answer D.

questions.prompt: A person saves money while planning for old age. Which function is money performing?
choices: Medium of exchange.
Standard of deferred payment.
Store of value.
Unit of account.
questions.explanation: Saving carries purchasing power into the future, so money acts as a store of value. Source: 0455_w23_11 Q11.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Original recent Paper 1 application; answer C.

questions.prompt: Money used to measure and repay a debt later acts as a standard of __________ payment.
questions.explanation: Standard of deferred payment is the function linked to borrowing, lending and future repayment.

quizzes.title: Money: characteristics and exam practice quiz
quizzes.description: Characteristics, their links to functions, and developed exam explanations.

questions.prompt: Which is not a function of money?
choices: Medium of exchange.
Portability.
Store of value.
Unit of account.
questions.explanation: Portability is a characteristic of effective money. The other three options are functions. Source: 0455_w24_11 Q10.

questions.prompt: Why do banknotes function as money?
choices: They are backed by gold.
They are durable.
They are generally acceptable.
They have intrinsic value.
questions.explanation: Durability helps a note circulate, but general acceptability is what allows it to settle payments. Source: 0455_w25_13 Q10.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Original recent Paper 1 hinge question; answer C.

questions.prompt: Money available in different denominations is __________, so it can be used for payments of different sizes.
questions.explanation: Divisibility means money can be split into smaller unit values. This is accepted Paper 2 mark-scheme language.

sources.label: Paper 2 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 2 mark scheme accepts divisible as a characteristic of money.

questions.prompt: Money needs to be limited in __________ so that it is scarce enough to retain value.
questions.explanation: Limited supply helps maintain scarcity and protects the store-of-value function.

sources.label: Paper 2 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 2 mark scheme accepts limited supply as a characteristic.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best develops the characteristic “coins are durable”?
choices: Coins are made in different denominations.
Coins are accepted because the government issues them.
Coins do not perish, so they can be reused and keep value over time.
Coins can be carried from one shop to another.
questions.explanation: Paper 2 awards the development mark for explaining how long life supports a money function, such as store of value. Source: 0455_w25_23 Q3(b).

sources.label: Paper 2 source
sources.note: Recent 4-mark explain question: one mark for each characteristic and one for each linked development.

quizzes.title: Macroeconomic aims quiz
quizzes.description: Check the six macroeconomic aims and common conflicts between them.

questions.prompt: Macroeconomic aims focus mainly on which level of the economy?
choices: The whole economy
One household only
One firm only
One product market only
questions.explanation: Macroeconomics studies economy-wide performance such as output, employment, inflation, and trade.

questions.prompt: Economic growth means an increase in real __________.
questions.explanation: Growth is usually measured by an increase in real GDP.

questions.prompt: Which aim is most directly linked to keeping inflation low and predictable?
choices: Stable prices
Full employment
Redistribution of income
Environmental sustainability
questions.explanation: Stable prices / low inflation means keeping the general price level rising slowly and predictably.

questions.prompt: Keeping unemployment low is the aim of full __________.
questions.explanation: Full employment means most people who are willing and able to work can find jobs.

questions.prompt: Which aim is most connected to avoiding persistent current account problems?
choices: Balance of payments stability
Stable prices
Redistribution of income
Economic growth
questions.explanation: Balance of payments stability means avoiding persistent current account deficits or surpluses.

questions.prompt: Reducing excessive income inequality is called redistribution of __________.
questions.explanation: Redistribution of income aims to reduce large gaps between high and low income groups.

questions.prompt: Why may economic growth conflict with environmental sustainability?
choices: More output may use more resources and create more pollution.
More output always reduces pollution.
Growth means imports must fall to zero.
Growth automatically makes income equal.
questions.explanation: Growth can create environmental costs if output rises through greater resource use or pollution.

questions.prompt: Higher employment may raise incomes, causing consumers to buy more imports and worsening the balance of __________.
questions.explanation: A rise in imports can worsen the current account position, affecting balance of payments stability.

quizzes.title: Government budget and spending quiz
quizzes.description: Check government budgets, budget balances, and the main areas, reasons and effects of government spending.

questions.prompt: Which definition best matches a government budget?
choices: A record of only the money spent by households and firms.
A policy that requires taxation to equal exports.
A plan or forecast for government revenue and government expenditure.
A measure of the difference between exports and imports.
questions.explanation: The syllabus definition is a plan or forecast for government revenue and expenditure.

questions.prompt: Government revenue is $780m and government expenditure is $780m. What is the budget position?
choices: $780m surplus
Balanced budget
$780m deficit
$1,560m balanced budget
questions.explanation: A balanced budget occurs when government revenue equals government expenditure.

questions.prompt: Tax revenue is $650m, other government revenue is $80m, and government expenditure is $790m. What is the budget balance?
choices: $60m surplus
$140m deficit
$60m deficit
$1,520m surplus
questions.explanation: Total revenue is $730m. $730m - $790m = -$60m, so spending exceeds revenue by $60m.

questions.prompt: When government expenditure is greater than government revenue, there is a budget __________.
questions.explanation: A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds government revenue.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only main areas of government spending in the syllabus?
choices: Exports, imports, profits, dividends, wages and rent.
Luxury goods, private profit, foreign holidays, shares and advertising.
Exchange rates, tariffs, quotas, imports and overseas investment.
Education, healthcare, infrastructure, welfare, defence and debt interest.
questions.explanation: Main areas include education, healthcare, infrastructure, welfare, defence and debt interest.

questions.prompt: Government spending on education and healthcare can increase access to __________ goods.
questions.explanation: Education and healthcare are merit goods that may be under-consumed without government support.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely long-run effect of government spending on roads, ports and communication networks?
choices: It immediately removes the need for taxation.
It can improve infrastructure, reduce costs for firms and increase productive capacity.
It guarantees that imports will fall to zero.
It means all public spending becomes welfare spending.
questions.explanation: Infrastructure spending can raise efficiency and productive capacity, supporting long-term economic growth.

questions.prompt: Government welfare benefits can help redistribute __________ and reduce poverty.
questions.explanation: Welfare benefits are transfer payments that can support lower-income households and reduce income inequality.

quizzes.title: Taxation foundations quiz
quizzes.description: Check reasons for taxation and direct and indirect tax examples.

questions.prompt: Why do governments collect taxes?
choices: To raise revenue for public spending.
To make every market private.
To remove the need for a budget.
To guarantee zero inflation.
questions.explanation: A main reason for taxation is to raise revenue to fund public services and other spending.

questions.prompt: A tax on cigarettes can be used to reduce consumption of a __________ good.
questions.explanation: Demerit goods create private or external costs, so governments may tax them to reduce consumption.

questions.prompt: Which is the best example of a direct tax?
choices: Income tax
Value added tax
Sales tax
Excise duty on cigarettes
questions.explanation: A direct tax is paid on income or wealth directly to government.

questions.prompt: A tax placed on spending on goods and services is an __________ tax.
questions.explanation: Indirect taxes are taxes on spending / goods and services.

questions.prompt: Corporation tax is a tax on what?
choices: Company profits
Household spending
Imported goods only
All public services
questions.explanation: Corporation tax is a direct tax on company profits.

questions.prompt: VAT and sales tax are usually examples of __________ taxes.
questions.explanation: VAT and sales tax are added to spending on goods and services.

questions.prompt: What is an import tariff?
choices: An indirect tax on imported goods.
A subsidy paid to all consumers.
A direct tax on company profits.
A benefit paid to unemployed workers.
questions.explanation: A tariff is an indirect tax on imports and can make imported goods more expensive.

questions.prompt: A pollution tax can encourage environmental __________.
questions.explanation: Pollution taxes raise the cost of polluting and can encourage environmental sustainability.

quizzes.title: Tax structures quiz
quizzes.description: Check progressive, regressive and proportional taxes.

questions.prompt: What happens in a progressive tax system?
choices: The percentage of income paid in tax rises as income rises.
Everyone pays exactly the same amount of tax.
Lower-income households always pay a higher percentage.
Only firms pay tax.
questions.explanation: Progressive taxes take a higher proportion from people with higher incomes.

questions.prompt: A tax where everyone pays the same percentage of income is called __________ tax.
questions.explanation: A proportional tax uses one constant tax rate.

questions.prompt: Why can an indirect tax be regressive?
choices: It may take a larger percentage of income from lower-income households.
It always makes rich people pay no tax.
It only applies to exports.
It must be paid directly from wages.
questions.explanation: The same tax on a product can be a larger share of a lower income.

questions.prompt: A household paying $500 tax from $10,000 income pays __________% of its income in tax.
questions.explanation: $500 divided by $10,000 is 0.05, or 5%.

questions.prompt: Progressive taxes can help redistribute __________ from higher-income to lower-income groups.
questions.explanation: Tax revenue can fund transfers or services that support lower-income households.

questions.prompt: In a progressive income tax, what happens when income moves into a higher band?
choices: The higher band is taxed at a higher marginal rate.
The person stops paying all tax.
Every household pays the same cash amount.
Only imported goods are taxed.
questions.explanation: A progressive income tax applies higher rates to higher income bands.

questions.prompt: Why should an answer classify a tax before explaining its effects?
choices: The type of tax affects who pays and how incentives change.
Classification means no explanation is needed.
All taxes have exactly the same effect.
Only direct taxes can raise revenue.
questions.explanation: Classifying the tax helps identify who pays, what price or income changes, and likely effects.

questions.prompt: A proportional tax charges the same __________ at all income levels.
questions.explanation: Proportional taxes keep the same percentage rate even when income differs.

quizzes.title: Expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy quiz
quizzes.description: Check fiscal policy, expansionary and contractionary measures, aggregate demand, employment and demand-pull inflationary pressure.

questions.prompt: What is fiscal policy?
choices: The use of government spending and taxation to influence economic activity and aggregate demand.
The use of interest rates by private banks only.
The buying and selling decisions of households.
The rules firms use to set wages.
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation to influence economic activity, aggregate demand and macroeconomic aims.

questions.prompt: Fiscal policy uses government spending and __________.
questions.explanation: Spending and taxation are the two main fiscal-policy instruments.

questions.prompt: Which is an expansionary fiscal policy?
choices: Increasing government spending or cutting taxes.
Cutting government spending and raising taxes.
Banning all imports.
Removing all public services.
questions.explanation: Expansionary policy raises aggregate demand by increasing spending or reducing taxes.

questions.prompt: Raising taxes or cutting government spending is usually __________ fiscal policy.
questions.explanation: Contractionary fiscal policy reduces aggregate demand and demand-pull inflationary pressure.

questions.prompt: Expansionary fiscal policy usually increases aggregate __________.
questions.explanation: Higher government spending or lower taxes can increase total spending in the economy.

questions.prompt: How can increased government spending reduce unemployment?
choices: It can raise demand for goods, services and labour.
It always reduces all prices instantly.
It stops firms from hiring workers.
It removes consumer spending from GDP.
questions.explanation: Higher spending can raise aggregate demand, output and derived demand for labour.

questions.prompt: Contractionary fiscal policy can reduce demand-pull inflationary __________.
questions.explanation: Lower aggregate demand can reduce demand-pull inflationary pressure.

questions.prompt: What is a likely short-run effect of cutting income tax?
choices: Households may have more disposable income and spend more.
Households must have less disposable income.
Government spending automatically becomes zero.
Exports must fall to zero.
questions.explanation: Lower income tax can raise disposable income, consumption and aggregate demand.

quizzes.title: Fiscal policy effects and limitations quiz
quizzes.description: Check fiscal-policy effects on macroeconomic aims and why the effects may be limited.

questions.prompt: Which option correctly matches a fiscal-policy change with the macroeconomic aim it is most likely to support?
choices: Higher progressive taxes and higher transfer payments - redistribution of income.
Higher government spending during inflation caused by excess demand - stable prices.
Lower environmental taxes on pollution - environmental sustainability.
Higher taxes during a recession - full employment through higher aggregate demand.
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy may support economic growth, full employment, stable prices, balance of payments stability, redistribution of income and environmental sustainability.

questions.prompt: Higher government spending may increase aggregate demand and real __________.
questions.explanation: If firms can raise output, higher demand may increase real GDP and economic growth.

questions.prompt: Which situation gives contractionary fiscal policy the strongest chance of reducing inflation?
choices: Inflation is mainly demand-pull and the economy is operating close to full capacity.
Inflation is mainly caused by higher imported oil prices and wages are unchanged.
Inflation is caused by reduced farm output after a drought.
Inflation is low because aggregate demand is weak and unemployment is rising.
questions.explanation: Higher taxes or lower government spending reduce aggregate demand most directly, so they are most effective against demand-pull inflation.

questions.prompt: Progressive taxes and transfer payments can reduce income __________.
questions.explanation: Progressive taxes take a larger share from higher incomes, while transfers can support lower-income households.

questions.prompt: Lower spending may reduce imports and support balance of payments __________.
questions.explanation: If consumers and firms buy fewer imported goods, international payments may become more stable.

questions.prompt: Which policy is most clearly designed to improve environmental sustainability through fiscal incentives?
choices: A pollution tax plus spending on renewable-energy infrastructure.
A cut in all tariffs, including tariffs on high-emission goods.
A reduction in unemployment benefits with no environmental condition.
A lower corporation tax for every firm regardless of pollution.
questions.explanation: Green spending and environmental taxes can change incentives and reduce pollution.

questions.prompt: Expansionary fiscal policy may have a weak response if consumer confidence remains __________.
questions.explanation: If confidence is low, households may save tax cuts rather than increase spending.

questions.prompt: An exam answer says: "Lower taxes will increase employment." Which improvement adds the best evaluation?
choices: Lower taxes may increase employment if confidence is high and extra spending is on domestic goods, but the effect can be weakened by saving, imports and time lags.
Lower taxes always increase employment because all households spend all extra income immediately.
Lower taxes cannot affect employment because taxation is not part of fiscal policy.
Lower taxes only affect environmental sustainability and never affect aggregate demand.
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy effects are conditional, so strong answers explain when the effect is likely or limited.

quizzes.title: Money supply and monetary policy quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 4.3.1: money supply, monetary policy measures and macroeconomic aims.

questions.prompt: What is the money supply?
choices: The total quantity of foreign currency available within the economy.
The total quantity of money available within the economy.
The total quantity of money issued by the central bank.
The total quantity of money within commercial banks.
questions.explanation: Money supply is the total quantity of money available within the economy, not just central-bank money or bank balances. Source: 0455_w24_12 Q18.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on money supply.

questions.prompt: The __________ is the amount of money in the economy.
questions.explanation: Money supply means the amount of money in an economy at a particular time.

questions.prompt: What is not normally a function of the central bank of a country?
choices: Acting as lender of last resort.
Issuing notes and coins.
Operating the government monetary policy.
Setting the government budget.
questions.explanation: The government budget is part of fiscal policy. Central banks may issue currency, act as lender of last resort and operate monetary policy. Source: 0455_w23_11 Q12.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on central-bank functions.

questions.prompt: Monetary policy often involves a change in which variables?
choices: Government expenditure or taxes.
Interest rates or the money supply.
Labour market or trade union laws.
Tariffs or quotas.
questions.explanation: Interest rates and money supply are monetary-policy variables. Source: 0455_s25_11 Q19.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on monetary-policy variables.

questions.prompt: Alongside interest rates and money supply, monetary policy can use __________ measures.
questions.explanation: Foreign exchange-rate measures are part of monetary policy in 4.3.1 and 4.3.2.

questions.prompt: What is not a monetary policy measure?
choices: Changes in income tax rates.
Changes in interest rates.
Changes in the exchange rate.
Changes in the money supply.
questions.explanation: Income tax is fiscal policy. Monetary policy can use interest rates, exchange-rate measures and money supply. Source: 0455_w25_11 Q19.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on monetary-policy measures.

questions.prompt: Monetary policy is used to influence __________.
questions.explanation: The syllabus says monetary policy influences macroeconomic aims.

questions.prompt: What correctly explains the effect of monetary policy measures on macroeconomic aims?
choices: A higher exchange rate will make imports more expensive and improve the balance of payments.
An increase in interest rates will encourage investment and lead to higher economic growth.
An increase in the money supply in an economy without spare capacity will result in demand-pull inflation.
Higher interest rates result in less income from savings and therefore higher unemployment.
questions.explanation: If money supply rises when spare capacity is absent, aggregate demand may rise faster than output and cause demand-pull inflation. Source: 0455_s24_13 Q19.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on monetary-policy effects.

quizzes.title: Interest rates quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 4.3.2: interest rates and their effects on spending, saving, borrowing, investment, output, employment and inflation.

questions.prompt: What is an interest rate?
choices: The cost of borrowing and reward for saving.
A tax on imports.
A government budget balance.
The number of workers unemployed.
questions.explanation: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, usually expressed as a percentage.

questions.prompt: A higher interest rate increases the __________.
questions.explanation: Higher rates make saving more attractive.

questions.prompt: A higher interest rate raises the __________.
questions.explanation: Higher rates make loans more expensive for households and firms.

questions.prompt: If interest rates fall, what is the most likely effect on saving and borrowing?
choices: Borrowing decreases; saving decreases.
Borrowing increases; saving decreases.
Borrowing decreases; saving increases.
Borrowing increases; saving increases.
questions.explanation: Lower rates make borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so borrowing is likely to rise while saving falls. Source: 0455_s25_11 Q11.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on lower interest rates, saving and borrowing.

questions.prompt: Which steps best explain how lower interest rates may increase employment?
choices: Lower rates -> cheaper borrowing -> higher spending and investment -> higher output -> higher employment.
Lower rates -> higher taxes -> lower demand -> higher employment.
Lower rates -> lower imports only -> higher employment.
Lower rates -> lower labour productivity -> higher employment.
questions.explanation: Lower interest rates can increase borrowing, spending, investment and output, so firms may hire more workers.

questions.prompt: Governments use monetary policy such as increasing the rate of interest. What is a result of increasing the rate of interest?
choices: It creates disincentives for wage earners.
It discourages investment by entrepreneurs.
It reduces the disposable income of consumers.
It reduces government transfer payments.
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates increase borrowing costs, so some entrepreneurs may delay or cancel investment. Source: 0455_m25_12 Q19.

sources.label: Paper 1 source
sources.note: Recent Paper 1 MCQ on increasing interest rates and investment.

questions.prompt: Higher interest rates may reduce demand-pull __________.
questions.explanation: Higher rates can reduce aggregate demand, lowering pressure on prices.

questions.prompt: What is one possible risk of higher interest rates?
choices: Output and employment may fall.
Borrowing must rise.
Demand-pull inflation must rise.
Saving becomes less rewarding.
questions.explanation: Higher rates can reduce spending and investment, so output and employment may fall.

quizzes.title: Money supply measures quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 4.3.2: money supply measures, with a brief foreign-exchange-rate definition check.

questions.prompt: What is the likely aim of increasing money supply?
choices: To reduce bank lending and aggregate demand.
To increase lending, spending, investment and output.
To increase income tax revenue.
To reduce the number of commercial banks.
questions.explanation: Increasing money supply can support lending, spending and investment.

questions.prompt: Increasing money supply may increase bank __________.
questions.explanation: More liquidity can support bank lending.

questions.prompt: More lending to firms may increase business __________.
questions.explanation: Firms may borrow to invest in capital equipment, branches or production.

questions.prompt: Reducing money supply is most likely to...
choices: increase demand-pull inflation.
reduce lending, spending and inflationary pressure.
increase the reward for saving directly.
raise government spending.
questions.explanation: Less money and lending can reduce spending pressure.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of increasing money supply too quickly when output cannot rise?
choices: Demand-pull inflation may rise.
Bank lending must fall.
Employment must fall immediately.
Exports must become cheaper.
questions.explanation: If extra demand grows faster than output, inflationary pressure may rise. Source: 2025FM-22 Q3(d).

sources.label: Paper 2 source
sources.note: Money-supply discussion includes demand, growth, employment and inflation risks.

questions.prompt: Which pair lists two monetary policy measures?
choices: Interest rates and money supply.
Income tax and government spending.
Minimum wages and public ownership.
Tariffs and subsidies.
questions.explanation: Past Paper 2 accepts interest rates and money supply as monetary-policy measures. Source: 2023ON-21 Q5(a).

questions.prompt: The __________ is the price of one currency in terms of another.
questions.explanation: This is only an introductory definition here; exchange rates are taught in detail in Unit 6.

questions.prompt: In this brief introduction, what happens when a country has a lower exchange rate?
choices: Exports may become cheaper for foreign buyers and imports may become more expensive.
Exports must become more expensive and imports must become cheaper.
Only government spending changes.
Only unemployment changes.
questions.explanation: This is the basic trade-price link. Detailed exchange-rate and current-account analysis comes later in Unit 6.

quizzes.title: Effects and limitations quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 4.3.3: macroeconomic effects, limitations and Paper 2 evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of expansionary monetary policy?
choices: Lower interest rates or increase the money supply.
Raise interest rates or reduce the money supply.
Raise income tax and reduce government spending.
Train workers to increase productive capacity.
questions.explanation: Expansionary monetary policy aims to raise aggregate demand.

questions.prompt: Which is the likely aim of contractionary monetary policy?
choices: To reduce aggregate demand and demand-pull inflationary pressure.
To increase aggregate demand and reduce saving.
To directly reduce all production costs.
To increase imports by increasing consumer spending.
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates or a lower money supply can reduce borrowing, spending, investment and aggregate demand.

questions.prompt: If higher aggregate demand causes firms to raise output and demand more labour, cyclical __________ may fall.
questions.explanation: Expansionary monetary policy may increase output and reduce cyclical unemployment when there is spare capacity.

questions.prompt: Why can a time lag limit monetary policy?
choices: Borrowing, spending, investment, output, cyclical unemployment and prices may adjust slowly.
Aggregate demand always changes before the central bank acts.
All households and firms must borrow immediately.
Imports and exports are not affected by aggregate demand.
questions.explanation: A policy change does not instantly change decisions across the economy.

questions.prompt: How can low consumer and business confidence limit lower interest rates?
choices: Households may save and firms may avoid borrowing for investment.
Households must spend more and firms must expand.
Cost-push inflation must fall to zero.
Imports must fall immediately.
questions.explanation: Confidence affects whether households and firms choose to spend, borrow and invest.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares demand-pull and cost-push inflation?
choices: Higher interest rates are stronger against demand-pull inflation than cost-push inflation from higher production costs.
Higher interest rates are equally strong against every cause of inflation.
Cost-push inflation is caused by too much aggregate demand.
Demand-pull inflation is caused only by higher fuel prices.
questions.explanation: Contractionary monetary policy reduces aggregate demand, but it may not remove higher production costs.

questions.prompt: How may an increase in the money supply benefit an economy?
choices: It may increase bank lending, spending, investment, aggregate demand, output and firm expansion.
It must reduce all prices immediately.
It must reduce imports immediately.
It directly increases income tax revenue.
questions.explanation: The 2025FM-22 mark scheme accepts higher lending, spending, investment, aggregate demand, growth and lower cyclical unemployment as benefits.

questions.prompt: Which risk was accepted in the 2025FM-22 Q3(d) mark scheme?
choices: Demand-pull inflation, more imports or household and firm debt.
Lower aggregate demand and lower output in every case.
A guaranteed fall in imports and prices.
No effect on bank lending or borrowing.
questions.explanation: The same limitations taught in the lesson appear in the mark-scheme points for the money-supply discuss question.

quizzes.title: Supply-side policy basics quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 4.4.1: supply-side policy, productive capacity, efficiency and long-run output.

questions.prompt: What is the main aim of supply-side policy?
choices: To increase productive capacity and total supply.
To reduce every firm's output.
To use only interest rates.
To increase imports without changing output.
questions.explanation: Supply-side policy aims to raise productive capacity, efficiency and long-run output.

questions.prompt: Supply-side policy aims to increase productive __________.
questions.explanation: Productive capacity is the economy's ability to produce goods and services.

questions.prompt: Which contrast is most accurate?
choices: Demand-side policy mainly affects aggregate demand; supply-side policy raises total supply.
Supply-side policy only changes consumer spending.
Monetary policy and supply-side policy use exactly the same measures.
Supply-side policy can only reduce output.
questions.explanation: The key exam contrast is aggregate demand versus total supply.

questions.prompt: Supply-side policies often have a stronger effect in the long __________.
questions.explanation: Training, infrastructure and investment may take time to affect output.

questions.prompt: How would higher productive capacity be shown on a PPC?
choices: A rightward shift of the PPC.
A movement from one point to another on the same PPC only.
A leftward shift caused by fewer resources.
No possible change.
questions.explanation: A rightward PPC shift shows greater productive capacity.

questions.prompt: Higher efficiency means less waste or more output from the same __________.
questions.explanation: Efficiency improves when inputs produce more output or less waste.

questions.prompt: Which pair shows the usual classification of supply-side policies?
choices: Interventionist and market-based.
Cash-only and barter-only.
Imports and exports only.
Private and impossible.
questions.explanation: Supply-side policies are often grouped into interventionist and market-based measures.

questions.prompt: Supply-side policy aims to increase total __________.
questions.explanation: The policy target is the economy's capacity to supply goods and services.

quizzes.title: Interventionist supply-side policies quiz
quizzes.description: Check government-led supply-side measures using education, training, healthcare, infrastructure and subsidies.

questions.prompt: Which is an interventionist supply-side policy?
choices: Government spending on education and training.
Privatising a state-owned firm.
Deregulating a market.
Reducing trade union power only.
questions.explanation: Interventionist supply-side policies use government spending or direct support to improve supply.

questions.prompt: What is productivity?
choices: Output per worker or per factor input.
The total number of shops in a city.
A tax on imports only.
The interest rate paid on savings.
questions.explanation: Productivity measures output per worker or input in a period of time.

questions.prompt: Training can increase workers' skills and __________.
questions.explanation: Training can make labour more productive and employable.

questions.prompt: Better healthcare can reduce working time lost through __________.
questions.explanation: Healthier workers may be absent less often and work more productively.

questions.prompt: Which measure can increase geographical labour mobility?
choices: Better transport links or housing access.
Banning workers from moving regions.
Removing all job adverts.
Reducing every worker's skills.
questions.explanation: Transport and housing can help workers reach jobs in different places.

questions.prompt: Training can improve occupational labour __________.
questions.explanation: Occupational mobility means workers can move between types of work.

questions.prompt: Which chain best explains an interventionist reduction in unemployment?
choices: Education -> higher skills -> workers match vacancies -> unemployment may fall.
Education -> lower skills -> fewer vacancies -> unemployment must fall.
Healthcare -> more illness -> productivity rises.
Transport worsens -> workers reach more jobs.
questions.explanation: The accepted chain links skills or mobility to employability and lower unemployment.

questions.prompt: Better infrastructure can reduce firms' transport __________.
questions.explanation: Infrastructure is an interventionist policy that can lower costs and raise capacity.

quizzes.title: Market-based supply-side policies quiz
quizzes.description: Check tax incentives, privatisation, deregulation and labour-market reforms.

questions.prompt: Which is a market-based supply-side policy?
choices: Deregulating a market to increase competition.
Government spending on healthcare.
Building a public road.
Subsidising training directly.
questions.explanation: Market-based policies work through incentives, competition and flexibility.

questions.prompt: Market-based policies rely on prices, profit and __________.
questions.explanation: The market-based route uses competition and incentives rather than direct provision.

questions.prompt: How can lower corporation tax raise productive capacity?
choices: It can increase retained profit and the incentive to invest.
It forces all firms to close.
It is direct public spending on roads.
It always reduces every firm's profit.
questions.explanation: More retained profit can fund investment in capital, technology or expansion.

questions.prompt: A lower corporation tax may increase firms' incentive to __________.
questions.explanation: Higher retained profit can encourage investment and expansion.

questions.prompt: What is privatisation?
choices: Transfer of assets from the public sector to the private sector.
An increase in government ownership of every firm.
A tax paid only by households.
A rise in unemployment benefits.
questions.explanation: Privatisation transfers assets or firms into private-sector ownership.

questions.prompt: Deregulation may reduce barriers to market __________.
questions.explanation: Lower entry barriers can increase competition and efficiency.

questions.prompt: Which is a possible risk of market-based supply-side reforms?
choices: Weaker worker or consumer protection.
Instant success in every industry.
No need to consider time lags.
No effect on incentives.
questions.explanation: Deregulation and labour-market reforms can improve efficiency but may reduce protection.

questions.prompt: Lower taxes can reduce government tax __________.
questions.explanation: This is one evaluation point for tax-cut supply-side policies.

quizzes.title: Supply-side effects and evaluation quiz
quizzes.description: Check syllabus 4.4.3: effects on growth, employment, prices, competitiveness and the current account.

questions.prompt: How can supply-side policy increase economic growth?
choices: By raising productive capacity and long-run output.
By permanently reducing every worker's skill.
By making firms unable to produce.
By lowering total supply.
questions.explanation: Supply-side policy can raise real GDP by increasing capacity and productivity.

questions.prompt: Higher productivity can reduce average production __________.
questions.explanation: Lower unit costs can reduce cost-push inflationary pressure.

questions.prompt: How can supply-side policy help price stability?
choices: Lower costs can reduce cost-push inflationary pressure.
Higher costs always reduce inflation.
Less output always means lower inflation with no risk.
It can only affect income tax revenue.
questions.explanation: Productivity gains can lower average costs and increase supply.

questions.prompt: If firms become more competitive, exports may __________.
questions.explanation: Lower prices or higher quality can raise export demand.

questions.prompt: Which chain links supply-side policy to the current account?
choices: Productivity rises -> costs fall -> exports become more competitive -> current account may improve.
Skills fall -> costs rise -> exports rise automatically.
Infrastructure worsens -> imports must disappear.
Workers train less -> current account must improve.
questions.explanation: Competitiveness is the key link to exports and the current account.

questions.prompt: Better skills and mobility may reduce structural __________.
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment falls when workers can match available jobs.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest evaluation point?
choices: Supply-side policies may take years and have opportunity cost.
Supply-side policies work instantly in every case.
Supply-side policies never need funding.
Supply-side policies cannot affect firms.
questions.explanation: Time lags and opportunity cost are core evaluation points.

questions.prompt: Money spent on training has an opportunity __________.
questions.explanation: Government spending on one policy cannot be used for another priority.

quizzes.title: Unit 1 Lesson 1 Quiz
quizzes.description: Retrieve the definitions, evidence and decisions used in the latest What is investment? lesson.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that a decision is a financial investment?
questions.zh: 什么证据最能表明一个决定属于金融投资？
choices: The asset has risen in price before
The main basis is expected income and/or evidence about underlying value, while possible loss is accepted
Money can be withdrawn immediately with no possible loss
The buyer plans to sell after an unverified rumour
questions.explanation: A financial investment seeks total return using income and/or evidence about value while possible loss remains.
questions.explanationZh: 金融投资以收入和/或价值证据为依据寻求总回报，同时仍有可能亏损。

questions.prompt: Which decision is saving rather than financial investment?
questions.zh: 哪一个决定属于储蓄，而不是金融投资？
choices: Keeping school-trip money in an easy-access account
Buying a diversified fund for long-term growth after reviewing its fees and risks
Buying shares for dividends and long-term value after analysing profits, debt and cash flow
Buying property mainly for expected net rental income
questions.explanation: The known near-term need makes liquidity and capital preservation decisive.
questions.explanationZh: 已知的近期需要使流动性和保本成为决定性因素。

questions.prompt: Which evidence most clearly indicates speculation?
questions.zh: 哪一项证据最清楚地表明属于投机？
choices: Expected bond interest after analysing credit risk
Expected net rental income after estimating vacancy and maintenance
Borrowing after a rumour of a next-week price jump and planning a quick sale
Accepting that a diversified fund held long term can lose value
questions.explanation: The decision depends mainly on a rumoured short-term price movement, and borrowing increases possible loss.
questions.explanationZh: 该决定主要依赖传闻中的短期价格变动，而且借款会增加潜在损失。

questions.prompt: Which statement about saving is correct?
questions.zh: 关于储蓄，哪一个陈述是正确的？
choices: Earning interest automatically changes saving into financial investment
Saving cannot lose purchasing power
Capital preservation and liquidity can matter more than a high return
Saving always means holding cash at home
questions.explanation: Saving can prioritise capital preservation and liquidity even when it earns interest.
questions.explanationZh: 即使获得利息，储蓄仍可优先考虑保本与流动性。

questions.prompt: Two people buy the same asset. Why might one be investing and the other speculating?
questions.zh: 两个人购买同一资产，为什么一个可能在投资，另一个可能在投机？
choices: The asset name decides the category
The person who pays the higher price is the speculator
The person planning to sell sooner is always the speculator
One bases expected return on income and/or evidence about long-term value; the other mainly on a price prediction
questions.explanation: Classification depends on the decision’s expected payoff basis and evidence, not only the asset name.
questions.explanationZh: 分类取决于决定的预期回报依据与证据，而不仅仅取决于资产名称。

questions.prompt: Which two components make up total return?
questions.zh: 总回报由哪两个部分构成？
choices: Liquidity and capital preservation
Income and the change in market value
Research and holding period
Interest and guaranteed profit
questions.explanation: Total return equals income plus the change in market value.
questions.explanationZh: 总回报等于收入加市场价值的变化。

questions.prompt: What did the historical household study illustrate about frequent trading?
questions.zh: 历史家庭研究说明频繁交易可能产生什么影响？
choices: Frequent trading guarantees a higher return
Every active trader loses all invested money
The market return is fixed each year
Trading costs can reduce net return
questions.explanation: In the historical sample, trading costs reduced the net return of the most-active group.
questions.explanationZh: 在该历史样本中，交易成本降低了交易最频繁群体的净回报。

questions.prompt: Nora borrows to buy shares after an unverified rumour. How can borrowing worsen the loss?
questions.zh: Nora听信未经证实的传闻，借钱买股票。借款会如何加重损失？
choices: The debt must still be repaid if the shares fall
Borrowing guarantees a higher selling price
The lender absorbs every market loss
Debt converts speculation into saving
questions.explanation: Nora remains responsible for repaying the borrowed money even if the asset loses value.
questions.explanationZh: 即使资产贬值，Nora仍有责任偿还借款。

quizzes.title: Unit 1 Lesson 2 Quiz
quizzes.description: Check whether students can define investment, return and financial goal, then choose and justify a clear next step for a family goal.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines investment?
questions.zh: 哪一个陈述正确定义了投资？
choices: Putting money into an asset to seek future return while accepting possible loss
Keeping all money unchanged until it is spent
Guaranteeing that money grows faster than prices
Choosing the investment with the highest recent return
questions.explanation: Investment seeks future return through an asset while retaining the possibility of loss.
questions.explanationZh: 投资通过资产寻求未来回报，同时仍存在可能损失。

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly completes the definition of return?
questions.zh: 哪一个陈述正确完成了回报的定义？
choices: Return is the income from an investment and cannot be negative.
Return is the gain or loss from an investment over a stated period, including price change and income.
Return is the original amount invested.
Return is any rise in price, regardless of income or costs.
questions.explanation: Return can be positive or negative and includes price change and income.
questions.explanationZh: 回报可以为正，也可以为负，并包括价格变化和收入。

questions.prompt: Which pair is included in the Lesson 2 definition of return?
questions.zh: 哪一组内容包含在第二课的回报定义中？
choices: Goal priority and age
Price change and income
Budget and tax
Investment name and popularity
questions.explanation: The course definition includes price change and income over a stated period.
questions.explanationZh: 课程定义包括规定期间内的价格变化和收入。

questions.prompt: Which description is a complete financial goal?
questions.zh: 哪一个描述是完整的财务目标？
choices: Make more money
Choose an investment soon
CNY 180,000 for university fees in six years, with high priority
Choose a high return
questions.explanation: A financial goal states a future use, amount, priority and time horizon.
questions.explanationZh: 财务目标说明资金的未来用途、金额、优先级和投资期限。

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest reason a family might invest?
questions.zh: 哪一个是家庭可能投资的最有力理由？
choices: To guarantee that every goal is reached
To avoid identifying when the money is needed
To copy an investment chosen by another family
To seek future return for a stated long-term goal while accepting possible loss
questions.explanation: The reason links investment to a stated goal, future return and possible loss.
questions.explanationZh: 该理由把投资与明确目标、未来回报和可能损失联系起来。

questions.prompt: What is the best next step for CNY 25,000 needed for a medical bill in four months?
questions.zh: 四个月后支付医疗账单所需的25,000元人民币，最佳下一步是什么？
choices: Keep it available because a loss or delay could leave the bill unpaid
Consider investing because every goal needs the highest possible return
Choose an investment before checking when the bill is due
Need more information because the purpose and date are unknown
questions.explanation: Choose ‘Keep available.’ The goal is near-term and urgent, so the money must be accessible and has little room for loss.
questions.explanationZh: 选择“保持资金可用”。该目标近期且紧急，因此资金必须可以使用，几乎没有承受损失的空间。

questions.prompt: A retirement goal is thirty years away. Which condition is still missing?
questions.zh: 退休目标在三十年后。仍然缺少哪一个条件？
choices: Proof that every return will be positive
The target amount and the family's ability to accept loss
A promise to choose one investment today
A list of classmates' opinions
questions.explanation: Choose ‘Need more information.’ A long horizon may support investment consideration, but the target amount and loss capacity are still missing.
questions.explanationZh: 选择“需要更多信息”。较长期限可能支持考虑投资，但仍缺少目标金额和损失承受能力。

questions.prompt: Why is ‘investing is simply a way to make more money’ incomplete?
questions.zh: 为什么“投资只是赚更多钱的一种方式”是不完整的？
choices: It contains too many financial conditions
It proves that investment is saving
It ignores the financial goal, time horizon, access need and possible loss
It explains the family goal fully
questions.explanation: A careful investment decision begins with the goal and its constraints, not return alone.
questions.explanationZh: 谨慎的投资决定从目标及其限制开始，而不是只看回报。

questions.prompt: What can general investor guidance not decide for a family?
questions.zh: 一般投资者指引不能替家庭决定什么？
choices: That investment involves risk
That goals have time horizons
That evidence should be checked
Its exact priorities, investment choice and whether a particular loss is acceptable
questions.explanation: General guidance supports a method, but family-specific priorities and constraints still require evidence.
questions.explanationZh: 一般指引支持一种方法，但家庭具体的优先级和限制仍需要证据。

questions.prompt: Which answer states a clear next step and justifies it with evidence?
questions.zh: 哪一个答案说明了清晰的下一步，并用证据加以说明？
choices: Consider investing for the stated long-term goal because urgent access is not needed; first check what loss could delay the goal.
Invest because returns are always positive.
Choose the most popular investment before setting a goal.
Avoid every investment because loss is possible.
questions.explanation: The answer names the next step, connects it to the goal and gives access and loss conditions.
questions.explanationZh: 该答案说明了下一步，把它与目标联系起来，并给出资金使用和损失条件。

quizzes.title: Unit 1 Lesson 3 Quiz
quizzes.description: Check whether students can classify goals by time horizon and liquidity need, then explain suitability without choosing a product first.

questions.prompt: What is time horizon?
questions.zh: 什么是投资期限？
choices: The period before invested money is expected to be needed
The number of products a family owns
The return earned last year
The date on which a product becomes popular
questions.explanation: Time horizon measures the period before the invested money is expected to be needed for the goal.
questions.explanationZh: 投资期限衡量预计需要为目标使用已投资资金之前的时间。

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines liquidity need?
questions.zh: 哪一个陈述正确定义了流动性需求？
choices: The need to earn the highest possible return
The need to own several different products
The need to access money quickly without accepting a large loss or delay
The need to predict next week's market price
questions.explanation: Liquidity need concerns reliable access without a large loss or delay.
questions.explanationZh: 流动性需求涉及无需承受重大损失或延迟即可可靠取用资金。

questions.prompt: Which factors belong in the Lesson 3 definition of suitability?
questions.zh: 哪些因素属于第三课的适合度定义？
choices: Product popularity, logo and advertising
Last week's price change only
The opinions of other families
Goal, horizon, liquidity need and ability to accept loss
questions.explanation: Suitability tests whether an investment matches the person's goal and constraints.
questions.explanationZh: 适合度检查投资是否与个人目标和限制相匹配。

questions.prompt: Which goal has the shortest horizon in the frozen profile?
questions.zh: 冻结资料中哪一个目标的期限最短？
choices: University fees beginning in three years
A home deposit in eight years
Retirement in thirty years
All three have the same horizon
questions.explanation: Three years is the shortest period before the money is expected to be needed.
questions.explanationZh: 三年是预计需要资金前最短的时间。

questions.prompt: Why does the home goal differ from the university goal?
questions.zh: 为什么住房目标与大学目标不同？
choices: It guarantees a higher return
It has a longer horizon and up to two years of date flexibility
It has no target amount
It requires money sooner
questions.explanation: The home goal is planned for eight years and its date can move, so its constraints differ from the fixed three-year education goal.
questions.explanationZh: 住房目标计划在八年后且日期可以调整，因此其限制不同于固定三年的教育目标。

questions.prompt: Which important facts are missing for the retirement goal?
questions.zh: 退休目标缺少哪些重要事实？
choices: Whether retirement is a future goal
Whether thirty years is longer than three years
The target amount, later withdrawal needs and ability to accept loss
Whether investment can involve return
questions.explanation: A long horizon alone is not enough to establish suitability.
questions.explanationZh: 仅凭较长期限不足以确定适合度。

questions.prompt: Why does the investment with the highest possible return not fit every goal?
questions.zh: 为什么可能回报最高的投资并不适合每一个目标？
choices: High possible return always means low risk
Every family has the same goal
Suitability depends only on recent performance
Goals have different horizons, liquidity needs and consequences of loss
questions.explanation: Return cannot establish suitability without the goal constraints.
questions.explanationZh: 如果没有目标限制，回报不能确定适合度。

questions.prompt: Which goal has the highest current liquidity need in the frozen profile?
questions.zh: 冻结资料中哪一个目标的当前流动性需求最高？
choices: University in three years with a fixed start date
Retirement in thirty years
Home deposit in eight years with date flexibility
All three have identical liquidity needs
questions.explanation: The earliest fixed payment date creates the strongest current need for reliable access.
questions.explanationZh: 最早且固定的付款日期形成最强的当前可靠取用资金需要。

questions.prompt: What can official time-horizon guidance not decide for the family?
questions.zh: 官方投资期限指引不能替家庭决定什么？
choices: That the period before a goal matters
A named product and whether its possible loss is acceptable for this family
That risk tolerance affects choices
That goals can have different horizons
questions.explanation: General guidance supports a method; family-specific suitability still requires evidence.
questions.explanationZh: 一般指引支持一种方法；家庭具体的适合度仍需要证据。

questions.prompt: Which explanation best shows why two goals require different investment choices?
questions.zh: 哪一个解释最能说明为什么两个目标需要不同的投资选择？
choices: Retirement is later, so any investment is suitable.
University is expensive, so it needs the highest possible return.
University money is needed sooner on a fixed date, while retirement money has a longer horizon and lower current access need; each choice must match its goal and loss capacity.
The same family should use one identical choice for all money.
questions.explanation: The answer compares horizon and liquidity need, then keeps the judgement conditional on suitability evidence.
questions.explanationZh: 该答案比较期限和流动性需求，并使判断以适合度证据为条件。
